title: Photographing Memory
content_html:
Photographing Memory

A photography project about memory can go in many directions - personal, collective, abstract, or even documentary. Photograph objects, places, or people iead to your own memories; traces of time-faded photos, worn clothing, childhood rooms, sites of remembrance (monuments, archives, abandoned buildings) that carry cultural memory. Everyday items can act as vessels of memory (a chair, a handwritten note, a toy). Certain landscapes (beaches, forests, cities) hold layers of history and collective experience.

Overlay past and present images (e.g., an old family photo aligned with its modern location), use blur, out-of-focus shots, or expired film to echo the fragility of memory. Shoot partial objects, cropped frames, or fragments of faces to reflect the incomplete nature of remembering. Combine your own photography with scans of old photos, letters, or diaries. Photograph empty spaces where something or someone used to be.

Pair each image with a memory fragment (your own or someone else’s words). Print on semi-transparent materials, layer them physically, or project onto walls to mimic how memory layers. Arrange photos in sequences that collapse time - childhood → present → imagined future. Let viewers handle, rearrange, or uncover images, simulating the act of remembering.

A still life series of objects may hold deep personal or family significance. Document locations from your past that are disappearing or changing, explore memories passed down through family stories, even those you never lived. Deliberately distort, fragment, or overexpose photos to question the reliability of memory. Capture places or traditions at risk of being forgotten, engaging with cultural or historical erasure.

Wetlands

Wetlands already embody layers of memory: they are ancient ecosystems, record-keepers of time (peat, pollen, sediments), and sites where fragility meets resilience. Turning photographs of wetland plants into a merged video ties the stillness of memory with the flow of time. Wetland plants hold memory of climate, water levels, and human presence; plants grow, decay, and return - mirroring how memory resurfaces and erodes. Wetlands are like living archives - every layer of vegetation, soil, and water tells a story.

Photograph individual wetland plants (reeds, rushes, sedges, mosses, water lilies) with attention to detail, texture, and light. Capture reflections, water ripples, fog, and shadows that suggest temporal shifts. If possible, photograph the same plants in different conditions (sun, mist, frost, drought). Cross-fade between plant portraits, so one form gradually becomes another - suggesting memory transforming. Overlap images with subtle opacity shifts, mimicking the layering of memories. Slow pacing (long dissolves, lingering shots) to let viewers feel memory’s slowness and fragility.

Stillness

A meditation on the stillness within wetlands - reflections on water, plants barely moving in wind, the quiet persistence of life. Long static photographs of single plants, slow dissolves with little to no movemen. Emphasis on mirrored surfaces and calm horizons. Stillness as the deep archive - the sediment of time holding memory in layers.

Simplicity

Strip away complexity - focus on elemental forms: water, plant, sky. Memory as simple, essential impressions that remain. Minimal compositions, few elements per frame. High contrast between plant silhouettes and water. Repetition of the same simple motif (e.g., a reed against open water). Memory as distilled essence - not the details, but the impression.

Change

Capture the Taoist principle of constant transformation - wetlands as shifting, alive, never the same twice. Photographs sequenced to show growth, decay, seasonal cycles. Faster dissolves, or morphing shapes to suggest constant movement Use wind and water ripples as metaphors for impermanence. Memory as fluid, never fixed - every recall reshapes the past.

This series of photographic video works explores memory through the Taoist principles of stillness, simplicity, and change. Each movement within the trilogy reflects a different way of understanding both the wetlands and the fragile, shifting terrain of remembrance.

Seen as a whole, the trilogy traces the rhythm of Tao:

stillness gives rise to simplicity,
simplicity opens into change, and
change returns to stillness.

Just as wetlands embody both permanence and flux, so too does memory - fragile, enduring, and endlessly transformed.

These 3 principles relate to the human psychology and brain functions of memory:

Psychological aspect

Memory requires moments of stillness. When we rest, daydream, or pause, the brain integrates experience into long-term memory. Quiet reflection also allows us to revisit and reinterpret past events. Human memory rarely stores every detail. Instead, it simplifies: we remember impressions, themes, and emotions more vividly than precise facts. This “essence” of experience is often what endures over time. Memory is not fixed. Every time we recall an event, we alter it slightly - influenced by our current mood, new experiences, and context. Memories are dynamic, continually rewritten.

Neuroscientific aspect
During sleep and restful states, the hippocampus “replays” experiences, strengthening neural connections - a process known as memory consolidation. Without stillness, memories remain fragmented or short-lived. The prefrontal cortex filters and reconstructs memories, discarding excess detail. This aligns with schema theory: memories are organized into simplified frameworks, so we can recall the gist quickly and efficiently. When recalled, a memory becomes malleable and can be reshaped before being stored again. Neural plasticity allows memory to adapt, but also makes it unreliable.

Parallel to wetlands
Just as sediment settles and preserves traces of the past, stillness in the mind preserves experience as memory. A reed silhouetted against water is like a distilled memory - stripped down to its most resonant form. A wetland is never the same twice - water levels rise and fall, plants shift with seasons. Likewise, memory flows, adapts, and transforms.

Stillness → preserving memory
Simplicity → distilling memory
Change → reshaping memory

What the Water Remembers

Memory, like a wetland, is layered, fragile, and alive. It does not exist as a fixed archive but as a living system, shaped by cycles of stillness, simplicity, and change. These three Taoist principles offer a lens through which to understand both the natural world and the inner landscape of the human mind.

In Taoist thought, stillness is not absence but presence - the quiet ground from which all things arise. Memory, too, depends on stillness. When the mind rests, when we sleep or drift into reverie, experiences settle like sediment in water. Neuroscience shows that the hippocampus replays and strengthens patterns of experience during sleep, consolidating them into long-term memory. Without stillness, recollection frays; with stillness, memory deepens. Wetlands embody this principle. Their waters hold time, preserving layers of organic matter that retain traces of what has passed. To stand among silent reeds is to sense the memory of centuries, held in still water and soil.

Taoism values the plain and unadorned, the return to simplicity. Human memory follows the same law. We do not recall every detail of an event; instead, we remember its essence. A fragment of light, a voice, the emotional contour - these are the impressions that endure. Psychologists describe this as schema: the brain distills complex experiences into simplified frameworks. What remains is not the photograph but the silhouette, not the exact words but the feeling. In this way, simplicity is the very shape of memory. Wetland plants mirror this: a single reed against water, stark and minimal, contains a world of associations. Simplicity clarifies what is essential, the way memory clarifies lived experience into meaning.

For Tao, the only constant is change. Memory is no different. Each time we recall, we alter the past. Neuroscience calls this reconsolidation: a memory becomes malleable when brought to mind, reshaped before being stored again. In this lies both fragility and resilience - memory is never fixed, yet it adapts and survives. Wetlands, too, are never the same twice. Water levels rise and fall, grasses bend and return, seasons transform the landscape. Memory flows in just this way: living, shifting, changing with the present moment.

Stillness, simplicity, and change form a cycle of memory, just as they form the rhythm of Tao and of wetlands themselves. The silent reed, the plain water, and the flowing grass are not only images of the natural world but metaphors for the human mind: how it preserves, distills, and transforms. To enter this work is to enter a landscape of remembering - one that is fragile, mutable, and alive. What the water remembers is also what we remember: that memory, like nature, is not an archive, but a living flow.

In stillness, memory settles like sediment. The mind, in rest and sleep, preserves what might otherwise be lost.
In simplicity, memory distills experience into essence: a fragment of light, a reed against water, the emotional shape of a moment.
In change, memory flows and reshapes. Each act of recall alters the past, just as wetlands shift with seasons and tides.

Taoism teaches that the world is defined by flow and transformation: wu wei (effortless action), ziran (naturalness), and the interplay of yin and yang. Nothing is static; stillness is only a moment within constant change. To “remember” in Taoist terms is not to fix the past, but to allow it to become part of the present flow. Thus, remembering is transformation: the past reshapes the present, and the present reshapes the meaning of the past.

Modern psychology shows that memory is reconstructive, not archival. Each act of recall changes the memory itself. Neuroscience calls this reconsolidation: once recalled, a memory is fragile, open to alteration before being stored again. Remembering, then, is not retrieval but transformation - a creative act of rewriting. Emotion and context re-colour what we recall, proving memory is not preservation, but living change.

Wetlands are landscapes of transformation. Plants grow, decay, and regenerate; water levels shift with tides and seasons; sediments layer and preserve while also decomposing. A wetland “remembers” through its ecology - pollen trapped in peat, seeds waiting in mud, traces of past climate stored in layers, yet those records are not fixed: they shift, erode, and reform. Like memory, wetlands embody both persistence and flux: they hold the past, but only as something in continual transformation.

Art is itself an act of remembering and transforming. An artist recalls, interprets, distills, and re-shapes experience into form. A photograph is not the past itself but a transformation of it - framed, selected, re-imagined. Still images of plants merge into video: memory becoming transformation in real time, the viewer’s act of interpretation is another layer: their memories infuse what they see, transforming the work further.

To Remember is to Transform

Memory is not a fixed archive but a living process. In Tao, all things flow and transform; stillness is only a moment within change. In psychology, every act of recall reshapes the past - memory is reconstruction, not preservation. Wetlands, too, embody this rhythm: they hold the traces of time in layers of water and soil, yet shift with tide, season, and growth. Art itself transforms experience into form, and in turn is transformed by those who encounter it. To remember is always to alter, to renew, to let the past live differently in the present.

A photograph is always a trace of the past, a “that-has-been.” It fixes a moment, yet in doing so it reminds us of loss and temporality. Photographs accumulate into archives of memory, shaping how both individuals and societies recall. A still photo is a frozen memory. Cinema uniquely captures duration and change - the “mummification of change” compared to photography’s frozen instant. Film is not just movement but time made visible; a direct image of temporality. When still photographs dissolve into moving sequence, they cross from fixed past → flowing present, embodying transformation.

Media doesn’t just record memory; it constructs and reshapes it. Photographic/video montage is one of the ways memory’s fluidity is enacted. video is memory unfolding, memory being reshaped each time it is recalled. The merging of still photographs into video enacts memory’s transformation in visual form. A photograph is often seen as a trace of the past - what Roland Barthes (1981) called the “that-has-been.” It freezes time, preserving a single moment as an index of what once was. In contrast, moving images open onto change and duration. André Bazin (1967) described cinema as the “mummification of change,” while Gilles Deleuze (1986, 1989) developed the idea of film as a direct image of time itself.

When still images are dissolved, layered, or sequenced into video, they cross from fixity into flow. Each transition mirrors the psychological and neurological process of memory reconsolidation: when we recall, we reshape. As Marita Sturken (1997) argues, media does not merely record memory but actively constructs and reconfigures it. Contemporary video artists such as Bill Viola have similarly employed slow dissolves and temporal layering to reveal memory as unfolding transformation.

Thus, the act of sequencing photographs into video is not simply formal but conceptual: it renders visible the way memory moves between preservation and change. To recall is to transform - and to merge the still with the moving is to show memory as a living process.
